docs.title: Kubernetes Networking Deep Dive
docs.text: Kubernetes networking is critical for SREs and system administrators. Pods must communicate with each other and with services, often across nodes.

docs.title: Kubernetes Networking Model
docs.text: Kubernetes uses a flat network model. Every Pod gets its own IP and can talk to other Pods directly.

docs.title: CNI (Container Network Interface)
docs.text:
CNI is the standard interface for networking in Kubernetes. Popular plugins: Cilium, Calico.

kubectl apply -f cni-config.yaml

docs.title: Example: Create a Pod
docs.text:
kubectl run nginx --image=nginx --restart=Never
kubectl get pods

Use kubectl describe pod nginx to inspect networking details.

docs.title: Kubernetes Network Policies: A Practical Troubleshooting Guide
docs.text:
Kubernetes NetworkPolicies help control communication between workloads. However, a policy that looks correct on paper can still result in unexpected connectivity failures when labels, selectors, ports, or CNI configuration do not match.

In this guide, we will work through a practical troubleshooting workflow for pod-to-pod communication, examine common policy mistakes, and explore how Cilium can help diagnose network issues.

docs.title: 1. Understand the traffic flow
docs.text: Start by identifying the source pod, destination pod, destination port, and namespace. Determine whether the traffic is governed by ingress or egress rules.

docs.title: 2. Inspect the policy
docs.text:
kubectl get networkpolicy -A
kubectl describe networkpolicy -n default
kubectl get pods -n default --show-labels

Check the selectors, namespace selectors, and allowed ports against the actual workloads.

docs.title: 3. Test connectivity
docs.text:
kubectl exec -it <source-pod> -- \
  curl -v --connect-timeout 5 http://<destination-service>:<port>

Compare the result before and after applying a policy. In a Cilium cluster, use Hubble flow visibility and Cilium endpoint information to investigate dropped traffic.

docs.title: 4. Troubleshooting checklist
docs.text:
• Verify pod labels and namespace selectors.
  • Confirm the destination port and protocol.
  • Check whether both ingress and egress policies apply.
  • Review CNI health and network-policy enforcement.
  • Use flow logs to distinguish a policy drop from routing or application failures.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: Troubleshoot Kubernetes networking layer by layer. Validate the policy, verify the endpoints, test the path, and use CNI-specific observability to identify where traffic is being dropped.

docs.title: Kubernetes Architecture
docs.text: Kubernetes is a set of cooperating control loops. You declare the desired state through the API, and controllers keep working until reality matches it.

docs.title: Control plane
docs.text: Component Role kube-apiserver The front door. Every read and write goes through it, and it authenticates, validates and persists requests. etcd Consistent key-value store that holds all cluster state. kube-scheduler Picks a node for each Pod that has none. kube-controller-manager Runs the controllers (Deployment, Node, Job and more) that reconcile state. cloud-controller-manager Talks to the cloud provider for load balancers, nodes and routes. Cloud clusters only.

docs.title: Node components
docs.text: Component Role kubelet Starts and monitors the Pods assigned to its node. Container runtime Runs the containers, usually containerd or CRI-O. kube-proxy Programs Service routing rules. Some CNIs replace it.

docs.title: What happens on kubectl apply
docs.text:
1. The API server authenticates the request, validates it and stores the object in etcd.
  2. The Deployment controller sees the new object and creates a ReplicaSet.
  3. The ReplicaSet controller creates Pod objects.
  4. The scheduler assigns each Pod to a node.
  5. The kubelet on that node asks the runtime to pull the image and start the containers.
  6. Readiness probes pass, and the Pod joins its Service endpoints.

docs.title: Quick health checks
docs.text:
kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose'
kubectl get nodes -o wide
kubectl -n kube-system get pods

docs.title: Kubernetes Deployments
docs.text:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nginx-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nginx
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:latest

docs.title: Pods
docs.text: A Pod is the smallest deployable unit: one or more containers that share a network namespace and storage.

docs.title: Lifecycle phases
docs.text: Phase Meaning Pending Accepted, but not yet running. Often waiting for a node, an image or a volume. Running Bound to a node with at least one container running. Succeeded All containers exited successfully. Typical for Jobs. Failed All containers ended and at least one failed. Unknown The node cannot be reached, so the state is not known.

docs.title: Probes
docs.text: Probe Question it answers If it fails startupProbe Has the app finished starting? Container is restarted. Other probes wait for it. readinessProbe Can it take traffic now? Removed from Service endpoints. livenessProbe Is it stuck? Container is restarted.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  containers:
    - name: web
      image: nginx:1.27
      ports:
        - containerPort: 80
      resources:
        requests: { cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi }
        limits:   { memory: 256Mi }
      startupProbe:
        httpGet: { path: /, port: 80 }
        periodSeconds: 2
        failureThreshold: 30
      readinessProbe:
        httpGet: { path: /, port: 80 }
        periodSeconds: 5
      livenessProbe:
        httpGet: { path: /, port: 80 }
        periodSeconds: 10
        failureThreshold: 3

Tip

Use a readiness probe on every service. Without it, traffic reaches Pods that are not ready yet. See Pod failures when something goes wrong.

docs.title: Requests vs limits
docs.text:
• Request: what the scheduler reserves for the container. It decides where the Pod fits.
  • Limit: the maximum the container may use.

CPU and memory behave differently when a limit is reached:

Resource At the limit CPU The container is throttled (slowed down). It keeps running. Memory The container is OOM-killed (exit code 137).

docs.title: QoS classes
docs.text:
Kubernetes assigns each Pod a class that decides eviction order under node pressure:

Class Rule Evicted Guaranteed Every container has CPU and memory requests equal to limits Last Burstable At least one request or limit is set Middle BestEffort Nothing set First 
kubectl get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='{.status.qosClass}'
kubectl top pod -n <namespace>        # needs metrics-server

docs.title: Guardrails per namespace
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: defaults
spec:
  limits:
    - type: Container
      defaultRequest: { cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi }
      default:        { memory: 256Mi }
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: team-quota
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "8"
    requests.memory: 16Gi
    pods: "50"

Tip

Set memory requests close to real usage and be careful with CPU limits. Tight CPU limits cause latency through throttling even when the node has spare capacity.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
A Secret holds small amounts of sensitive data such as passwords, tokens and keys.

Warning

Secret values are base64 encoded, not encrypted. Anyone who can read the Secret can decode it. Protect them with RBAC and encryption at rest.

docs.title: Create and read
docs.text:
kubectl create secret generic db-credentials \
  --from-literal=username=app \
  --from-literal=password='CHANGE_ME'

kubectl get secret db-credentials -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d

docs.title: Use in a Pod
docs.text:
env:
  - name: DB_PASSWORD
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef:
        name: db-credentials
        key: password

Mounting a Secret as a volume is usually preferable to environment variables. Mounted files can update without a restart, and values are less likely to leak into logs and crash dumps.

docs.title: Good practice
docs.text:
• Restrict get, list and watch on Secrets with RBAC. list also exposes values.
  • Turn on encryption at rest for Secrets in etcd.
  • Never commit Secret manifests to Git. Use an external secrets operator, sealed secrets or SOPS.
  • Rotate credentials, and prefer short-lived ones where possible.

More in Cluster Hardening.

docs.title: Kubernetes Service Example
docs.text:
kubectl expose pod nginx --type=NodePort --port=80
kubectl get svc

docs.title: StatefulSet
docs.text:
Use a StatefulSet when each replica needs a stable identity and its own storage, such as databases and queues. Pods get ordered names (db-0, db-1) and keep their volumes across restarts.

apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: db
spec:
  clusterIP: None          # headless: gives each Pod its own DNS record
  selector: { app: db }
  ports:
    - port: 5432
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: db
spec:
  serviceName: db
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: db }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: db }
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: db
          image: postgres:16
          volumeMounts:
            - { name: data, mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data }
  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - metadata:
        name: data
      spec:
        accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
        resources:
          requests: { storage: 10Gi }

docs.title: Job and CronJob
docs.text:
A Job runs a task to completion. A CronJob creates Jobs on a schedule.

apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: nightly-backup
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid          # never overlap runs
  successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  failedJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      backoffLimit: 2
      template:
        spec:
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
          containers:
            - name: backup
              image: busybox:1.36
              command: ["sh", "-c", "echo running backup"]

Note

A StatefulSet is not a backup strategy. Replicated storage does not protect you from deleting data, so test restores regularly (see Disaster Recovery).

docs.title: Volumes and Persistent Storage
docs.text: Object What it is PersistentVolume (PV) A piece of storage in the cluster. PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) A request for storage by a workload. StorageClass A template for dynamically provisioning PVs.

docs.title: Access modes
docs.text: Mode Meaning ReadWriteOnce (RWO) Mounted read-write by one node ReadOnlyMany (ROX) Mounted read-only by many nodes ReadWriteMany (RWX) Mounted read-write by many nodes (needs a supporting backend) ReadWriteOncePod (RWOP) Read-write by a single Pod

docs.title: Example claim
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: data
spec:
  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
  storageClassName: standard      # use a class from: kubectl get storageclass
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 10Gi

docs.title: Things worth knowing
docs.text:
• With volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer, a PVC stays Pending until a Pod uses it. That is normal.
  • reclaimPolicy: Delete removes the underlying disk when the PVC is deleted. Use Retain for data you cannot lose.
  • Growing a volume needs allowVolumeExpansion: true on the StorageClass.
kubectl get pvc,pv -A
kubectl describe pvc <name>

Having trouble? See Storage troubleshooting.

docs.title: Kubernetes Troubleshooting
docs.text: Debug failed pods and services.

docs.title: Pod Networking and CNI
docs.text: The Container Network Interface (CNI) plugin gives each Pod an IP and connects it to the rest of the cluster. Kubernetes defines the rules, and the CNI plugin implements them.

docs.title: Common plugins
docs.text: Plugin Notes Cilium eBPF-based. Can replace kube-proxy, with rich policy and observability. Calico Mature, with strong network policy. Supports BGP routing or overlays. Flannel Simple overlay. Does not enforce NetworkPolicy by itself. AWS VPC CNI Pods get real VPC IPs. Pod density depends on ENI limits.

docs.title: Overlay vs routed
docs.text:
• Overlay (VXLAN, IP-in-IP) wraps Pod traffic in node-to-node packets. It is easy to set up and works almost anywhere, with some encapsulation overhead.
  • Routed (BGP or cloud routes) uses real routes. It is faster and easier to inspect, but needs network support.

docs.title: How Services are implemented
docs.text:
kube-proxy programs rules on every node so that traffic to a Service IP reaches one of its Pods:

  • iptables mode is the common default.
  • IPVS mode scales better for very large Service counts.
  • eBPF (for example Cilium) can replace kube-proxy entirely.

docs.title: Useful checks
docs.text:
kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,CIDR:.spec.podCIDR
kubectl get pods -A -o wide
ls /etc/cni/net.d/                      # run on a node

Warning

NetworkPolicy only works if your CNI enforces it. Creating policies on a CNI that ignores them gives a false sense of security.

docs.title: DNS in Kubernetes (CoreDNS)
docs.text: CoreDNS runs in kube-system and answers every name lookup inside the cluster.

docs.title: Names you can use
docs.text:
Name Resolves to my-svc Service in the same namespace my-svc.my-ns Service in another namespace my-svc.my-ns.svc.cluster.local Fully qualified name pod-0.my-svc.my-ns.svc.cluster.local A StatefulSet Pod behind a headless Service

A headless Service (clusterIP: None) returns the Pod IPs directly instead of one virtual IP.

docs.title: The ndots:5 surprise
docs.text:
Pods get a resolver setting ndots:5. Any name with fewer than five dots is tried with each search suffix first, so an external lookup like api.example.com can cost several failed queries before it succeeds.

Reduce the noise per Pod:

spec:
  dnsConfig:
    options:
      - name: ndots
        value: "2"

Alternatively, use a trailing dot (api.example.com.) to skip the search list.

docs.title: Debugging
docs.text:
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l k8s-app=kube-dns
kubectl -n kube-system logs -l k8s-app=kube-dns --tail=50

kubectl run dns-test --rm -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- bash
# inside the pod:
nslookup kubernetes.default
cat /etc/resolv.conf

If lookups fail, see Services and DNS troubleshooting.

docs.title: Gateway API and Ingress
docs.text:
Both bring HTTP and HTTPS traffic from outside the cluster to your Services. A controller or implementation must be installed, since creating the objects alone does nothing.

ingress-nginx is retired

The community ingress-nginx controller was retired in March 2026 and no longer receives fixes. Check whether you run it:

    kubectl get pods --all-namespaces --selector app.kubernetes.io/name=ingress-nginx

The Ingress API itself still exists, but the Kubernetes project recommends **Gateway API** as the successor.

docs.title: Gateway API
docs.text:
Gateway API separates responsibilities: infrastructure teams own the Gateway, and application teams own HTTPRoutes.

apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: my-app
spec:
  gatewayClassName: example-class     # provided by your Gateway implementation
  listeners:
    - name: https
      protocol: HTTPS
      port: 443
      hostname: app.example.com
      tls:
        mode: Terminate
        certificateRefs:
          - name: app-example-com-tls
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: app
  namespace: my-app
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - name: web
  hostnames: ["app.example.com"]
  rules:
    - matches:
        - path: { type: PathPrefix, value: / }
      backendRefs:
        - name: app
          port: 80

For a Gateway shared across namespaces, set allowedRoutes on the listener to control which namespaces may attach routes.

docs.title: Ingress (if you still use it)
docs.text:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: app
  namespace: my-app
spec:
  ingressClassName: <your-controller-class>
  tls:
    - hosts: [app.example.com]
      secretName: app-example-com-tls
  rules:
    - host: app.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: app
                port: { number: 80 }

docs.title: Migrating
docs.text: The Kubernetes project provides an Ingress2Gateway tool that converts existing Ingress resources to Gateway API objects. Treat its output as a first draft, then test routing, TLS and any annotation-based behaviour in a non-production cluster.

docs.title: Network Policies
docs.text: By default every Pod can talk to every other Pod. NetworkPolicy restricts that, but only if your CNI enforces it.

docs.title: How they behave
docs.text:
• Policies are allow-lists that add together. There are no deny rules.
  • Once any policy selects a Pod for a direction (ingress or egress), that direction becomes default-deny for that Pod. Only what a policy allows gets through.

docs.title: 1. Start from default-deny
docs.text:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all
  namespace: my-app
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]

docs.title: 2. Allow DNS
docs.text:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-dns-egress
  namespace: my-app
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
          podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              k8s-app: kube-dns
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }

docs.title: 3. Allow only what is needed
docs.text:
Frontend to backend on port 8080:

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: backend-from-frontend
  namespace: my-app
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app: backend }
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app: frontend }
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }

Remember that the frontend also needs an egress rule to reach the backend while default-deny egress is on.

docs.title: Test it
docs.text:
kubectl run probe --rm -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot -n my-app -- \
  curl -sS -m 3 http://backend:8080/healthz

See also Cluster Hardening.

docs.title: Kubernetes Networking Overview
docs.text: Kubernetes networking looks complicated because several layers cooperate. Each layer has one job, and most problems are easier once you know which layer you are in.

docs.title: The network model
docs.text:
1. Every Pod gets its own IP address.
  2. Pods can talk to all other Pods without NAT.
  3. Node agents can talk to all Pods on their node.
  4. A Service gives a stable virtual IP and DNS name to a changing set of Pods.

For a longer walkthrough, read the article Kubernetes Networking Deep Dive.

When something is broken, go straight to Services and DNS troubleshooting.

docs.title: GitOps
docs.text: GitOps keeps the desired state of your systems in Git and uses an agent in the cluster to make reality match it. Every change is a reviewed commit, so you get an audit trail, easy rollbacks and no manual kubectl apply from laptops.

docs.title: Example: an Argo CD Application
docs.text:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: demo
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/example/demo-config.git
    targetRevision: main
    path: deploy
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: demo
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true

prune removes resources that were deleted from Git, and selfHeal reverts manual changes made directly in the cluster.

docs.title: Pitfalls to plan for
docs.text:
• Secrets: never commit plain secrets. Use an external secrets operator or sealed secrets.
  • Drift alerts: decide who gets notified when a sync fails.
  • Repository layout: separate application code from environment configuration so promotions are simple.

docs.title: Platform Engineering
docs.text: Platform engineering builds an internal platform so product teams can ship without becoming Kubernetes experts. Instead of every team solving deployment, observability and security on its own, a platform team provides paved roads that are self-service, secure by default and supported.

docs.title: Core ideas
docs.text:
• Internal Developer Platform (IDP): the set of tools and workflows developers use to build, deploy and run software.
  • Golden paths: opinionated, well-supported ways to do common things, such as creating a new service.
  • Self-service: developers get what they need without opening a ticket.
  • Platform as a product: the platform has users, a roadmap and feedback loops.

docs.title: Typical building blocks
docs.text: Concern Common tools Delivery Argo CD, Flux Policy and guardrails Kyverno, OPA Gatekeeper Observability Prometheus, Grafana, OpenTelemetry Infrastructure provisioning Crossplane, Terraform Developer portal Backstage

docs.title: How to know it's working
docs.text:
Track adoption of the golden paths, deployment lead time, change failure rate and developer satisfaction. A platform nobody chooses to use is not succeeding, however well engineered.

Next: GitOps with Argo CD.

docs.title: Go for SRE
docs.text: Go compiles to a single static binary that is easy to ship, which makes it ideal for small operational tools. It is also the language of Kubernetes, so reading its source and writing controllers or operators becomes natural.

docs.title: Example: a tiny HTTP health checker
docs.text:
package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    if len(os.Args) < 2 {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "usage: healthcheck <url>")
        os.Exit(2)
    }

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 5*time.Second)
    defer cancel()

    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, os.Args[1], nil)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(2)
    }

    start := time.Now()
    resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "FAIL:", err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()

    fmt.Printf("%s -> %d in %v\n", os.Args[1], resp.StatusCode, time.Since(start).Round(time.Millisecond))
    if resp.StatusCode >= 400 {
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

Build it with go build -o healthcheck . and the exit code makes it easy to use in scripts and CI.

docs.title: Programming for SRE
docs.text:
Operations work gets safer and faster when repeated tasks become code. Two languages cover most of what I use day to day:

  • Python: quick automation, glue scripts, data wrangling and API clients.
  • Go: fast, single-binary tools, and the language Kubernetes and most cloud native projects are written in.

docs.title: Python for SRE
docs.text: Python is the fastest route from idea to working automation. With the official Kubernetes client you can query a cluster in a few lines.

docs.title: Example: find pods that are not healthy
docs.text:
pip install kubernetes

from kubernetes import client, config

config.load_kube_config()          # use load_incluster_config() inside a cluster
v1 = client.CoreV1Api()

for pod in v1.list_pod_for_all_namespaces().items:
    if pod.status.phase not in ("Running", "Succeeded"):
        print(f"{pod.metadata.namespace}/{pod.metadata.name}: {pod.status.phase}")

docs.title: Habits that keep scripts safe
docs.text:
• Use a virtual environment and pinned dependencies.
  • Make scripts read-only by default and require an explicit flag for changes.
  • Log what you did, and handle API errors instead of ignoring them.

docs.title: AWS Certification Roadmap
docs.text: AWS groups certifications into four levels. Confirm the current list and exam codes at aws.amazon.com/certification, since exams are refreshed and renamed regularly.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Solutions Architect Associate is the strongest first "real" AWS exam, because it teaches the services everything else builds on.
  • Specialty and Professional exams assume real hands-on time, so build things in a sandbox account.
  • Pair AWS with a CNCF certification such as CKA to cover Amazon EKS properly.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Role-based Microsoft certifications expire after one year, but renewal is a free online assessment. Fundamentals do not expire.
  • AZ-104 is a prerequisite for the Expert certifications, so it keeps paying off.

docs.text: Google Cloud has three levels. Confirm the current list at cloud.google.com/learn/certification, because exams are revised often.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• The Associate Cloud Engineer exam rewards comfort with the gcloud command line, so practise there, not just in the console.
  • Associate and Professional certifications are valid for about two years, so plan renewals.
  • GKE appears across several exams, which makes CKA a natural companion.

docs.title: Golden Kubestronaut Path
docs.text:
Golden Kubestronaut is CNCF's highest recognition. It requires every CNCF certification plus the Linux Foundation's LFCS, and once earned it is yours for life. The list grows as CNCF adds certifications, so check the official program page before you plan.

At the time of writing, that is 15 CNCF certifications plus LFCS.

docs.title: What you need beyond Kubestronaut
docs.text:
You already have the five Kubernetes certifications (CKA, CKAD, CKS, KCNA, KCSA). The rest, grouped by theme:

Theme Exam Observability PCA: Prometheus Certified Associate OTCA: OpenTelemetry Certified Associate Networking and mesh CCA: Cilium Certified Associate ICA: Istio Certified Associate GitOps and delivery CAPA: Certified Argo Project Associate CGOA: Certified GitOps Associate Platform engineering CBA: Certified Backstage Associate CNPA: Certified Cloud Native Platform Engineering Associate CNPE: Certified Cloud Native Platform Engineer Policy KCA: Kyverno Certified Associate Linux LFCS: Linux Foundation Certified System Administrator

docs.title: A sensible order
docs.text:
1. LFCS to anchor the Linux foundation.
  2. PCA and OTCA for observability, since SRE work depends on them.
  3. CGOA then CAPA for GitOps and Argo.
  4. KCA, CCA and ICA for policy, networking and mesh.
  5. CBA, CNPA and CNPE for platform engineering.

Tip

Pair each exam with a small real project, such as an Argo CD setup or a Prometheus alert rule. You keep the skill long after the exam.

Related topics on this site: Platform, Security and SRE.

docs.title: CNCF Kubestronaut Path
docs.text: Kubestronaut is awarded to people who pass all five CNCF Kubernetes certifications. Official details: CNCF Kubestronaut program.

docs.title: Recommended order
docs.text: Step Exam Format Why this order 1 KCNA: Kubernetes and Cloud Native Associate Multiple choice Builds the vocabulary and the big picture 2 KCSA: Kubernetes and Cloud Native Security Associate Multiple choice Security concepts that make CKS easier 3 CKA: Certified Kubernetes Administrator Hands-on The core operations skill set 4 CKAD: Certified Kubernetes Application Developer Hands-on Speed with workloads and manifests 5 CKS: Certified Kubernetes Security Specialist Hands-on The hardest, and it requires a current CKA

docs.title: How I'd prepare
docs.text:
• Live in a cluster. Build one with kubeadm, break it, and fix it. The Troubleshooting section is a good drill list.
  • Get fast with kubectl. Imperative commands, --dry-run=client -o yaml, and kubectl explain save minutes.
  • Use the practice simulator that comes with exam registration, and review the candidate handbook for what is allowed.
  • Study concepts, not exam content. Sharing real exam questions breaks the candidate agreement.

docs.title: After the five
docs.text: Everything must stay current to keep the Kubestronaut title, so plan renewals. The next step is the Golden Kubestronaut.

docs.title: Certification Roadmaps
docs.text: Certifications are useful when they prove hands-on skill, so I recommend them by the work you want to do, not by the logo.

docs.title: How to choose
docs.text:
1. Pick the role first. SRE, platform, security and architecture each reward different exams.
  2. Prefer hands-on exams. A live-terminal exam is much harder to pass without real skill.
  3. Pair one vendor-neutral certification with one cloud. For example, CKA plus AWS or Google Cloud.
  4. Plan renewals. Every credential expires, and some programs change their exam lineup often.

docs.title: Typical validity
docs.text:
Always confirm on the vendor's site, because rules change.

Program Typical validity CNCF / Linux Foundation Varies by exam AWS 3 years Google Cloud 2 years (Associate and Professional) Microsoft Azure Role-based: 1 year with free online renewal; fundamentals do not expire Red Hat 3 years

docs.title: Suggested paths by goal
docs.text: Goal Start with SRE / DevOps CKA, then a cloud DevOps credential (AWS DevOps Pro or Google Cloud DevOps Engineer) Platform engineering CKA and CKAD, then the CNCF platform and GitOps exams Security KCSA, then CKS, then a cloud or vendor-neutral security certification Cloud architecture A cloud Associate, then the matching Professional or Expert

docs.text:
• CNCF Kubestronaut and Golden Kubestronaut
  • AWS, Google Cloud and Azure
  • Security certifications

docs.title: Security Certification Roadmap
docs.text: Security credentials fall into a few families. Choose by whether you defend clusters, clouds, or organisations.

docs.title: Cloud-native and Linux
docs.text: Certification Focus KCSA: Kubernetes and Cloud Native Security Associate Concepts and threat models CKS: Certified Kubernetes Security Specialist Hands-on cluster hardening (requires a current CKA) Red Hat Certified Specialist in Security: Linux (EX415) Hardening and compliance on RHEL

docs.title: A cloud-native security path
docs.text:
1. KCSA for concepts.
  2. CKS for hands-on hardening.
  3. A cloud security specialty for your main provider.
  4. CCSP or CISSP once you have the experience, to broaden into architecture and governance.

Related topics on this site: Cluster Hardening and Network Policies.

docs.title: Cluster Hardening Checklist
docs.text: A practical baseline for any production cluster.

docs.title: 1. Least-privilege RBAC
docs.text: Avoid binding cluster-admin to people or workloads. Grant namespaced roles with only the verbs and resources needed, and review bindings regularly.

docs.title: 2. Enforce Pod Security Standards
docs.text:
Label namespaces so the built-in admission controller applies the restricted profile. Try warn first to see what would break:

kubectl label namespace my-app pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted
kubectl label namespace my-app pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted

docs.title: 3. Default-deny network policy
docs.text:
Start from "no traffic" and allow only what is required:

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all
  namespace: my-app
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress
    - Egress

Warning

Denying all egress also blocks DNS. Add a policy that allows traffic to your cluster DNS service.

docs.title: 4. Protect secrets
docs.text: Enable encryption at rest for Secrets in etcd, restrict who can read them, and prefer an external secret manager for sensitive credentials.

docs.title: 5. Secure images
docs.text: Scan images in CI, pin by digest rather than mutable tags, and sign images you build.

docs.title: 6. Log and patch
docs.text: Enable API server audit logging, keep Kubernetes and node operating systems patched, and restrict access to etcd and the kubelet API.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: Security works best as part of the design, not as a review at the end. Kubernetes documentation describes defence in depth as four layers, often called the 4Cs: Cloud, Cluster, Container and Code. A weakness in an inner layer is much harder to exploit when the outer layers are sound.

docs.title: What I cover here
docs.text:
• Hardening clusters: RBAC, Pod Security Standards, network policies and secrets.
  • Securing the software supply chain: image scanning, signing and provenance.
  • Detection and response: audit logs and runtime monitoring.

Start with the cluster hardening checklist.

docs.title: Alerting
docs.text: Best practices for SRE alerting.

docs.title: Capacity Planning
docs.text: Capacity planning makes sure the service has enough resources for today's demand and a safe margin for tomorrow's.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Measure demand: requests per second, data growth, peak versus average.
  2. Know the limits: load test to find where latency or errors start to climb.
  3. Forecast: use growth trends and known events such as launches and sales.
  4. Keep headroom: plan for peaks and for losing a node or zone (N+1).
  5. Review regularly, and tie it to cost.

docs.title: The USE method
docs.text:
For every resource (CPU, memory, disk, network), check:

  • Utilization: how busy it is.
  • Saturation: how much work is waiting.
  • Errors: how often it fails.

Saturation is the early warning that utilisation alone hides.

docs.title: Autoscaling on Kubernetes
docs.text:
Tool Scales HPA Pod replicas, based on metrics VPA Pod resource requests Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter Nodes

Autoscaling reacts to load but does not replace planning. Limits, quotas and node supply still apply. See Requests, Limits and QoS.

docs.title: Disaster Recovery
docs.text: Plan and execute DR drills.

docs.title: Incident Management
docs.text: An incident is any event that hurts users or the business. A clear process lets people act calmly instead of improvising under pressure.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
1. Detect: an alert or a user report.
  2. Triage: assess impact and set a severity.
  3. Mitigate: stop the harm first. Rollback, fail over or scale. Root cause comes later.
  4. Communicate: keep stakeholders informed on a regular rhythm.
  5. Resolve: confirm recovery against the SLI.
  6. Learn: hold a postmortem.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
Role Job Incident commander Coordinates and decides. Does not debug. Operations lead Investigates and applies fixes. Communications lead Updates stakeholders and customers. Scribe Keeps the timeline.

Small teams combine roles, but someone must own coordination.

docs.title: Example severity levels
docs.text:
Adapt these to your organisation:

Level Meaning SEV1 Major outage or data loss. All hands. SEV2 Significant degradation for many users. SEV3 Limited impact. Handle in working hours.

docs.title: First ten minutes
docs.text:
• Open one channel and name an incident commander.
  • State impact and the time it started.
  • Check recent changes first. They explain most incidents.
  • Prefer rollback to a risky live fix.
  • Post an update, and then keep to a schedule.

For hands-on diagnosis see Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Healthy on-call
docs.text: Keep rotations sustainable, make handoffs explicit, and keep runbooks next to the alerts they explain. Every page should be actionable, or the alert should change.

docs.title: What is SRE?
docs.text: Site Reliability Engineering applies software engineering to operations. Reliability becomes a feature that is measured, budgeted and engineered, instead of something achieved by heroics.

docs.title: Core principles
docs.text:
• Reliability is a product feature. Users feel availability and latency, not your architecture.
  • Measure it with SLOs. Agree on a target for what "reliable enough" means.
  • Spend an error budget. The gap between the SLO and 100% is room for change and risk.
  • Eliminate toil. Automate repetitive manual work.
  • Learn from failure. Run blameless postmortems and fix systemic causes.
  • Keep it simple. Complexity is the main enemy of reliability.

docs.title: SRE, DevOps and platform engineering
docs.text:
Main question Typical output DevOps How do we ship quickly and safely together? Culture, CI/CD, shared ownership SRE Is the service reliable enough, and how do we prove it? SLOs, error budgets, on-call, postmortems Platform engineering How do we make good practice the easy path? Internal platform and golden paths

They overlap heavily, and good teams use all three ideas.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
1. SLIs, SLOs and error budgets
  2. Monitoring and alerting
  3. Incident management and postmortems
  4. Reliability patterns, capacity planning and disaster recovery
  5. Toil and automation and release engineering

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text: Prometheus, Grafana, and alerting strategies.

docs.title: Postmortems
docs.text: A postmortem is a written record of an incident that turns pain into improvement. The aim is to fix systems, not to find someone to blame.

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
• Blameless. Assume everyone acted sensibly with the information they had.
  • Systemic. Ask why the system allowed the mistake, not who made it.
  • Timely. Write it while memory is fresh.
  • Shared. Learning that stays in one team is wasted.

docs.title: Template
docs.text:
1. Summary: what happened, in two or three sentences.
  2. Impact: who and what was affected, for how long, and the error budget used.
  3. Timeline: key events with timestamps.
  4. Root causes and contributing factors: use "why" chains, not a single cause.
  5. What went well and what went badly.
  6. Action items: each with an owner, a priority and a due date.

docs.title: Good action items
docs.text:
Weak Strong "Be more careful with config changes" "Add a validation step in CI that blocks invalid config (owner, due date)" "Improve monitoring" "Alert on the queue depth SLI, with a runbook"

Prefer actions that remove the failure mode over actions that depend on people remembering.

Tip

Review old postmortems for repeat themes. Repeats show where the real investment belongs.

docs.title: Release Engineering
docs.text: Most incidents follow a change, so safe releases are one of the best reliability investments.

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
• Small, frequent changes are easier to understand and roll back.
  • Automate the path to production, and review everything through GitOps where you can.
  • Release progressively, and watch the SLIs while you do.
  • Make rollback fast and boring.

docs.title: Strategies
docs.text: Strategy How it works Rolling update Replace Pods gradually (the Kubernetes default). Canary Send a small share of traffic to the new version first. Blue/green Run two environments and switch traffic. Feature flags Ship code dark and enable it separately.

docs.title: Safe rolling updates
docs.text:
strategy:
  type: RollingUpdate
  rollingUpdate:
    maxUnavailable: 0
    maxSurge: 25%

kubectl rollout status deploy/api
kubectl rollout undo deploy/api

docs.title: Measure delivery
docs.text:
The DORA metrics are a good scorecard: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, and time to recover from a failed deployment.

Tie release speed to the error budget: when the budget is healthy, release more freely.

docs.title: In application code
docs.text:
Pattern What it does Timeouts Never wait forever on a dependency. Retries with backoff and jitter Recover from brief faults without causing a retry storm. Circuit breakers Stop calling a failing dependency so it can recover. Bulkheads Isolate resources so one failure does not take everything down. Load shedding Reject excess work early to protect the core. Graceful degradation Serve a reduced experience instead of failing. Idempotency Make retries safe.

Warning

Retries multiply load. Without backoff, jitter and a retry budget, they can turn a small problem into an outage.

docs.title: On Kubernetes
docs.text:
Spread replicas across failure domains and protect them during maintenance:

apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: api }

In the Pod template of the Deployment:

topologySpreadConstraints:
  - maxSkew: 1
    topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
    whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
    labelSelector:
      matchLabels: { app: api }

Also use readiness probes, sensible resource requests, and disaster recovery plans that you actually test.

docs.title: SLIs, SLOs and Error Budgets
docs.text: Term Meaning Example SLI A measurement of service behaviour Share of requests that succeed SLO The target for that measurement over a window 99.9% over 30 days SLA A contract with consequences if you miss it Service credits Error budget Allowed unreliability: 100% minus the SLO 0.1% of requests

docs.title: What an SLO allows
docs.text:
Over 30 days:

SLO Allowed downtime 99% 7.2 hours 99.5% 3.6 hours 99.9% 43.2 minutes 99.95% 21.6 minutes 99.99% 4.3 minutes

Each extra nine costs much more to deliver, so choose the target users actually need.

docs.title: Example SLI (Prometheus)
docs.text:
sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api",code!~"5.."}[5m]))
/
sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api"}[5m]))

docs.title: Using the budget
docs.text: Agree on an error budget policy in advance. While budget remains, ship features. When it is spent, slow down and invest in reliability. That turns "stability versus speed" arguments into a shared, data-driven rule.

docs.title: Alert on burn rate
docs.text:
Page on how fast the budget is being consumed, not on raw error spikes:

Window Burn rate Budget consumed Action 1 hour (and 5 minutes) 14.4 2% Page 6 hours (and 30 minutes) 6 5% Page 3 days (and 6 hours) 1 10% Ticket 
- alert: ApiFastBurn
  expr: |
    (
      sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api",code=~"5.."}[1h]))
      / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api"}[1h])) > (14.4 * 0.001)
    )
    and
    (
      sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api",code=~"5.."}[5m]))
      / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api"}[5m])) > (14.4 * 0.001)
    )
  labels:
    severity: page

The example assumes a 99.9% SLO, so 0.001 is the error budget. More in Alerting.

docs.title: Toil and Automation
docs.text: Toil is operational work that is manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical, without lasting value, and that grows in proportion to the service. Handling it forever keeps a team too busy to improve anything.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: A common SRE guideline is to keep toil under about half of the team's time, so the rest goes to engineering that reduces future work.

docs.title: Finding toil
docs.text:
• Review tickets and pages for repeated tasks.
  • Ask the team what they dread doing.
  • Track time spent, even roughly.

docs.title: The automation ladder
docs.text:
1. Document it as a runbook.
  2. Script it so a person runs one command.
  3. Make it self-service so users do it themselves.
  4. Make it self-healing so the system does it automatically.

docs.title: Example: from runbook to script
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -Eeuo pipefail
ns="${1:?usage: restart-unhealthy.sh <namespace>}"

kubectl get pods -n "$ns" --no-headers \
  | awk '$3 == "CrashLoopBackOff" {print $1}' \
  | while read -r pod; do
      echo "Deleting $pod"
      kubectl delete pod "$pod" -n "$ns"
    done

Note

A script that hides a recurring failure is not a fix. Track why it keeps happening and remove the cause.

See also Shell and Ansible and GitOps.

docs.title: Safe shell scripts
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -Eeuo pipefail
trap 'echo "failed at line $LINENO" >&2' ERR

threshold="${1:-85}"
df -P -x tmpfs -x devtmpfs | awk -v t="$threshold" '
  NR > 1 { gsub("%", "", $5); if ($5 + 0 >= t) printf "%s is at %s%%\n", $6, $5 }
'
  • set -Eeuo pipefail stops on errors, unset variables and failed pipes.
  • Quote variables and validate input.
  • Run scripts through shellcheck before you trust them.

docs.title: cron and timers
docs.text:
crontab -e
# m h dom mon dow  command
0 2 * * *  /usr/local/bin/backup.sh >> /var/log/backup.log 2>&1

Prefer systemd timers when you want logging, dependency handling and catch-up of missed runs.

docs.title: Ansible: describe the state, not the steps
docs.text:
# site.yml
- hosts: all
  become: true
  tasks:
    - name: Ensure chrony is installed
      ansible.builtin.dnf:
        name: chrony
        state: present

    - name: Ensure chronyd is enabled and running
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: chronyd
        state: started
        enabled: true

ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini site.yml --check --diff    # preview first
ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini site.yml

Good playbooks are idempotent, so running them twice changes nothing the second time. For the bigger picture see Toil and Automation.

docs.title: The boot sequence
docs.text:
1. Firmware (UEFI or BIOS) finds a boot device.
  2. Bootloader (GRUB2) loads the kernel and the initramfs.
  3. Kernel starts and mounts the root filesystem.
  4. systemd starts services up to the default target.

docs.title: Find out why a boot failed
docs.text:
journalctl -b -1 -p err         # previous boot errors
systemctl --failed

docs.title: Recovery targets
docs.text:
sudo systemctl rescue           # single-user, with basic services
sudo systemctl emergency        # minimal shell with the root filesystem

A common cause of a failed boot is a bad /etc/fstab entry. Fix it from the emergency shell and test with mount -a.

docs.title: Reset a lost root password (RHEL 8 and 9)
docs.text:
Only do this on systems you are authorised to administer, with console access.

  1. At the GRUB menu press e, add rd.break to the end of the linux line, then press Ctrl+x.
  2. In the emergency shell:
mount -o remount,rw /sysroot
chroot /sysroot
passwd root
touch /.autorelabel          # fixes SELinux labels on the next boot
exit
exit

Tip

Protect your systems from this by securing console and bootloader access, and by using disk encryption where appropriate.

docs.title: Inspect
docs.text:
ip -br a                    # addresses
ip r                        # routes
ss -tulpn                   # listening ports and owning processes
nmcli device status         # NetworkManager (RHEL)
resolvectl status           # DNS (systemd-resolved systems)

docs.title: Troubleshooting ladder
docs.text:
Work from the bottom up and stop at the first failure:

Layer Check Link ip link, cable or virtual NIC state Address ip a Route ip r, then ping <gateway> DNS dig example.com, getent hosts example.com Port ss -tulpn, curl -v http://host:port Firewall firewall-cmd --list-all Application logs with journalctl

docs.title: firewalld
docs.text:
sudo firewall-cmd --get-active-zones
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=https
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-port=8443/tcp
sudo firewall-cmd --reload
sudo firewall-cmd --list-all

Without --permanent, a change is lost at reload or reboot. Keep the default policy closed and open only what you need.

docs.title: Packet capture
docs.text:
sudo tcpdump -ni eth0 port 443 -c 20

Typical clues: repeated SYNs without replies suggest a firewall or routing issue. Resets suggest nothing is listening.

For the Kubernetes layers see K8s Networking.

docs.title: Performance Troubleshooting
docs.text: When a server is slow, take a structured first look instead of guessing.

docs.title: The first 60 seconds
docs.text:
uptime                  # load averages
dmesg -T | tail         # kernel errors, OOM kills
vmstat 1                # run queue, memory, swap, CPU split
mpstat -P ALL 1         # per-CPU balance
pidstat 1               # per-process CPU
iostat -xz 1            # disk latency and utilisation
free -m                 # memory and swap
sar -n DEV 1            # network throughput
top                     # the overall picture

Some tools come from the sysstat package.

docs.title: How to read it
docs.text: Signal What it suggests Load far above CPU count CPU contention or processes blocked on I/O High %iowait or disk await Slow or saturated disk Swap in and out activity Memory pressure us high Application CPU use sy high Kernel work: syscalls, networking, interrupts

docs.title: Out of memory
docs.text:
dmesg -T | grep -i 'killed process'
journalctl -k | grep -i oom

The kernel OOM killer picks a victim when memory runs out. Check whether it was a memory leak or a limit set too low.

docs.title: Think in USE terms
docs.text: For each resource, look at **U**tilization, **S**aturation and **E**rrors. See Capacity Planning.

docs.title: SELinux: fix it, do not disable it
docs.text:
getenforce
sudo ausearch -m avc -ts recent          # recent denials
ls -Z /var/www/html                      # file labels

Common fixes:

sudo restorecon -Rv /srv/app                                   # reset labels
sudo semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/srv/app(/.*)?"
sudo restorecon -Rv /srv/app
sudo semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8081               # allow a custom port
getsebool -a | grep httpd
sudo setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on                 # persistent boolean

Setting SELinux to permissive helps you diagnose, but running it permanently disabled removes a strong layer of defence.

docs.title: SSH
docs.text:
In /etc/ssh/sshd_config (or a drop-in under sshd_config.d/):

PermitRootLogin no
PasswordAuthentication no
PubkeyAuthentication yes

sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl reload sshd     # validate, then apply

Keep a second session open while you test, so you cannot lock yourself out.

docs.title: Baseline checklist
docs.text:
• Keep packages patched (dnf-automatic can automate security updates).
  • Run firewalld with a closed default (networking).
  • Use auditd to record sensitive events.
  • Remove unused services and accounts.
  • Scan against a benchmark with OpenSCAP (oscap) and the CIS benchmarks.
  • Centralise and protect logs.

See also Users and Permissions and Cluster Hardening.

docs.title: Disks, Filesystems and LVM
docs.text:
LVM puts a flexible layer between disks and filesystems, so you can grow storage without downtime.

Warning

pvcreate and mkfs destroy existing data. Check the device with lsblk first.

docs.title: Add a new disk with LVM
docs.text:
lsblk -f
sudo pvcreate /dev/sdb
sudo vgcreate vg_data /dev/sdb
sudo lvcreate -n lv_app -L 20G vg_data
sudo mkfs.xfs /dev/vg_data/lv_app

sudo mkdir -p /srv/app
sudo blkid /dev/vg_data/lv_app                       # note the UUID
echo 'UUID=<uuid>  /srv/app  xfs  defaults,nofail  0 0' | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab
sudo mount -a && df -hT /srv/app

Use the UUID in /etc/fstab, since device names can change. Always run mount -a after editing, or a typo can break the next boot.

docs.title: Grow a volume
docs.text:
sudo vgs                                              # free space in the group
sudo lvextend -r -L +10G /dev/vg_data/lv_app          # -r also grows the filesystem

XFS can grow but cannot shrink. ext4 can do both, with resize2fs.

docs.title: Health checks
docs.text:
df -h                  # space
df -i                  # inodes (a full inode table looks like a full disk)
lsblk
sudo lvs && sudo vgs && sudo pvs

For Kubernetes volumes see Persistent Storage.

docs.title: Everyday commands
docs.text:
systemctl status nginx
sudo systemctl enable --now nginx
sudo systemctl restart nginx
systemctl list-units --failed
sudo systemctl daemon-reload          # after editing unit files

docs.title: Logs with journalctl
docs.text:
journalctl -u nginx -f                       # follow
journalctl -u nginx --since "1 hour ago"
journalctl -p err -b                         # errors since boot
journalctl -b -1                             # previous boot

docs.title: A service unit with sensible hardening
docs.text:
/etc/systemd/system/demo-api.service

[Unit]
Description=Demo API
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
User=demo
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/demo-api
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5
NoNewPrivileges=true
ProtectSystem=strict
ProtectHome=true
PrivateTmp=true
ReadWritePaths=/var/lib/demo

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

docs.title: Timers (a modern cron)
docs.text:
backup.timer

[Timer]
OnCalendar=*-*-* 02:00:00
Persistent=true

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target

It runs a matching backup.service. Check with systemctl list-timers. Persistent=true runs a missed job after downtime.

docs.title: Slow boots
docs.text:
systemd-analyze blame | head
systemd-analyze critical-chain

docs.title: Users and groups
docs.text:
sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash alice
sudo passwd alice
sudo usermod -aG wheel alice        # RHEL: wheel. Debian/Ubuntu: sudo
id alice
sudo chage -l alice                 # password ageing
sudo usermod -L alice               # lock the account

docs.title: File permissions
docs.text:
Digit Meaning 4 read (r) 2 write (w) 1 execute (x) 
chmod 640 app.conf                  # owner rw, group r, others none
chmod u+x deploy.sh
sudo chown app:app /var/lib/app
umask 027                           # default: new files not readable by others

docs.title: Special bits
docs.text: Bit Effect setuid (u+s) Runs with the file owner's privileges. Use sparingly. setgid (g+s) on a directory New files inherit the directory's group. sticky (+t) Only the owner can delete files, as on /tmp.

docs.title: ACLs
docs.text:
For access beyond owner, group and others:

setfacl -m u:bob:rw report.txt
getfacl report.txt

docs.title: sudo
docs.text:
sudo visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/ops

%ops ALL=(root) /usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx

Grant specific commands, not blanket ALL, and review who has access. More in SELinux and Hardening.

docs.title: Services and DNS Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Work from the client towards the server, and stop at the first layer that fails.

 DNS  →  Service  →  Endpoints  →  Pod  →  NetworkPolicy  →  Ingress/Gateway

docs.title: DNS lookups fail
docs.text:
kubectl run dns-test --rm -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- nslookup kubernetes.default
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l k8s-app=kube-dns
kubectl -n kube-system logs -l k8s-app=kube-dns --tail=50
  • CoreDNS Pods not running or crash-looping.
  • A default-deny egress policy that does not allow DNS (fix).
  • Slow lookups from ndots:5. See DNS.

docs.title: Service has no endpoints
docs.text:
This is the most common cause of "the Service does not work".

kubectl get svc <svc> -n <ns>
kubectl get endpointslices -n <ns> -l kubernetes.io/service-name=<svc>
kubectl get pods -n <ns> --show-labels
  • The Service selector does not match the Pod labels.
  • Pods are not Ready, because the readiness probe is failing.
  • targetPort does not match the port the container listens on.

docs.title: Reaching it still fails
docs.text:
Test directly at each hop:

kubectl port-forward pod/<pod> 8080:<container-port> -n <ns>     # bypass the Service
kubectl run probe --rm -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot -n <ns> -- \
  curl -sS -m 3 http://<svc>:<port>

If the Pod works but the Service does not, look at selectors and ports. If both work from one Pod and not another, suspect a NetworkPolicy.

docs.title: NetworkPolicy blocking traffic
docs.text:
kubectl get networkpolicy -n <ns>
kubectl describe networkpolicy <name> -n <ns>

Remember that default-deny needs both an egress rule on the caller and an ingress rule on the target.

docs.title: Ingress or Gateway errors
Node Problems
docs.text:
kubectl get nodes -o wide
kubectl describe node <node>        # check Conditions and Events

docs.title: Conditions to read
docs.text: Condition Healthy value Problem means Ready True Kubelet cannot report healthy MemoryPressure False Node is low on memory, so Pods may be evicted DiskPressure False Disk or inode shortage, often from images and logs PIDPressure False Too many processes

docs.title: NotReady
docs.text:
Log in to the node and check, in this order:

systemctl status kubelet
journalctl -u kubelet -n 100 --no-pager
systemctl status containerd
crictl ps
df -h && free -m

Common causes:

  • The kubelet or container runtime stopped.
  • Expired kubelet or cluster certificates.
  • The CNI plugin is not ready, which shows in the node's Ready condition message.
  • A full disk.
  • Lost connectivity to the API server.

docs.title: Maintaining a node safely
docs.text:
kubectl cordon <node>                                  # stop new Pods
kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
kubectl uncordon <node>                                # when done

Tip

PodDisruptionBudgets can block a drain. If it hangs, check kubectl get pdb -A before forcing anything.

docs.title: Troubleshooting: Start Here
docs.text: Most incidents are solved faster by following the same steps every time than by guessing.

docs.title: A repeatable method
docs.text:
1. Define the symptom. What exactly is failing, for whom, and since when?
  2. Check what changed. Deployments, config, node upgrades and certificate expiry cause most outages.
  3. Walk the layers from the outside in: DNS, then Service, then endpoints, then Pod, then node.
  4. Gather evidence before you change anything: events, logs and describe output.
  5. Change one thing at a time, and note what you did.

docs.title: The five commands I reach for first
docs.text:
kubectl get pods -A -o wide
kubectl describe pod <pod> -n <ns>
kubectl logs <pod> -n <ns> --previous
kubectl get events -n <ns> --sort-by=.lastTimestamp
kubectl debug -it <pod> -n <ns> --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=<container>

describe and events explain most scheduling, image and probe failures. --previous shows the logs of the container that just crashed. kubectl debug attaches a temporary toolbox container to a live Pod.

docs.title: Which page do I need?
docs.text: What you see Go to Pending, ImagePullBackOff, CrashLoopBackOff, OOMKilled Pod failures Node NotReady, pressure conditions Nodes Service unreachable, DNS errors, 502/503 Services and DNS PVC Pending, volume mount errors Storage Just want the commands Quick Reference

docs.title: Pod Failures
docs.text:
Start every investigation with:

kubectl describe pod <pod> -n <ns>      # read the Events at the bottom

docs.title: Pending
docs.text:
The Pod was accepted but cannot start yet.

  • Events say 0/N nodes are available. Insufficient CPU or memory, taints without tolerations, or a nodeSelector or affinity that matches nothing.
  • PVC not bound. See Storage.
  • Quota exceeded. Check kubectl describe resourcequota -n <ns>.

docs.title: ImagePullBackOff
docs.text:
• A typo in the image name or tag.
  • A private registry without imagePullSecrets.
  • Registry rate limits or network access from the node.
kubectl describe pod <pod> | grep -A5 Events

docs.title: CrashLoopBackOff
docs.text:
The container starts, exits, and Kubernetes keeps restarting it with growing delays.

kubectl logs <pod> -n <ns> --previous
kubectl get pod <pod> -n <ns> \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].lastState.terminated}'
Exit code Usual meaning 1 Application error. Read the logs. 137 Killed (SIGKILL). Often an OOM kill. 143 Terminated (SIGTERM). Check shutdown handling.

Common causes: missing config or Secret, wrong command, a liveness probe that fails too early (add a startupProbe), or a dependency that is not ready.

docs.title: OOMKilled
docs.text:
kubectl get pod <pod> -n <ns> \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].lastState.terminated.reason}'

If it prints OOMKilled, raise the memory limit, or find the leak. See Requests, Limits and QoS.

docs.title: CreateContainerConfigError
docs.text: A referenced ConfigMap or Secret key does not exist, or the name is wrong. describe names the missing object.

docs.title: Running but not Ready
docs.text:
The readiness probe is failing. Check the probe path and port, then run it by hand:

kubectl exec <pod> -n <ns> -- wget -qO- http://localhost:8080/healthz

docs.title: Evicted
docs.text: The node ran short of memory, disk or PIDs. See Nodes, and set realistic requests so important Pods are not first in line.

docs.title: Storage Troubleshooting
docs.text:
kubectl get pvc,pv -A
kubectl describe pvc <name> -n <ns>
kubectl get storageclass

docs.title: PVC stuck in Pending
docs.text:
• WaitForFirstConsumer is normal until a Pod that uses the claim is scheduled.
  • No default StorageClass, or the storageClassName is wrong.
  • The provisioner or CSI driver is failing. Check its Pods in kube-system.
  • Not enough capacity or quota.

docs.title: Multi-Attach error
docs.text: A ReadWriteOnce volume is still attached to another node, which often happens after a node failure. Wait for the detach, or confirm the old Pod is gone. Do not force-detach until you are sure nothing is writing to the disk.

docs.title: Mount or permission errors
docs.text:
• Check that the Pod is in the same zone as a zonal disk.
  • If the app cannot write, set securityContext.fsGroup so the volume is group-writable.

docs.title: Volume full or needs to grow
docs.text:
kubectl exec <pod> -n <ns> -- df -h
kubectl patch pvc <name> -n <ns> -p '{"spec":{"resources":{"requests":{"storage":"20Gi"}}}}'

Expansion requires allowVolumeExpansion: true on the StorageClass, and you can only grow, never shrink.

Background: Volumes and Persistent Storage.
